newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU wheat tax move seen as first step to exports.
newsitem.headline: EU wheat tax move seen as first step to exports.

text.p: Thursday's decision to abolish wheat export taxes is a first step by the European Union towards resuming stalled exports, a French grain trader said on Friday.
But EU wheat is not yet competitive and needs the help of subsidies to start flowing abroad again.

"It is a signal. Above all it gives us perspective and allows us to say that the Commission will be involved on the market again," Bernard Valluis, managing director of Soufflet Trading, told Reuters.
"It means that from today there is a willingness on the part of the EU to participate in the world market," he said.
The EU on Thursday scrapped export taxes for all types of wheat and wheat flour or semolina and replaced them with short validity licences that have no fixed value.
"We're still out of line (with the world market)," Valluis said.
"The Commission knows this. But the transition away from the kind of situation we were in always happens gradually."

Grain officials have said the "nil value" licence procedure adopted by the EU -- a riskier venture for traders than licences which can be fixed at zero tax or subsidy -- is an interim step towards resuming full-blown exports once the harvest arrives.
But to export more than symbolic quantities the EU will have to go back to probably double-digit Ecu refunds, they said.
Valluis said Thursday's move would give the industry a clearer climate in which to prepare new grain export deals.

Official figures released earlier showed small quantities of wheat had already left the EU using the five Ecu per tonne tax before it was abolished but these were limited to around 1,000 tonnes. Part of this was thought to be in truckloads between France and Switzerland.
Traders are now waiting for the EU to open its weekly export tenders, at which they can bid for variable subsidies, in order to start the mainstream exports flowing again.
The Commission has said tenders could be opened towards the end of June, but the EU would be in no hurry to accept the tender bids and actually start exporting.
